analysis.one_liner: Takes congressional map-drawing away from state legislators and gives it to independent citizen commissions.
analysis.headline: The bill to end gerrymandering by independent redistricting commissions died in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single Republican cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state to redraw its congressional districts through an independent commission instead of the state legislature. Commissions could not consider voters' party affiliation or where incumbents live, had to keep counties and communities together, and had to hold public meetings and publish maps and data online. States would also be barred from redrawing maps mid-decade for political gain, and would receive federal money per House seat to run the commission. It never received a hearing or vote in the House Judiciary Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, especially in states where one party draws congressional maps to lock in its own seats. Districts would have to follow county and neighborhood lines, ignore partisan voting data and incumbent addresses, and be drawn in public, making seats more responsive to actual election results.

how_it_helps.text: Redistricting would be done by an independent commission whose members cannot have held office, run for office, or worked for a party or candidate in the previous four years, and who must promise not to run for Congress until after the next census [S3].

Commission members may not consider voters' party affiliation, voting history, or the residence of incumbent House members when drawing districts, except as needed to comply with the Voting Rights Act [S3].
Districts must be contiguous and compact and, to the extent practicable, keep counties, municipalities, and neighborhoods whole [S3].
Commissions must hold all meetings in public, maintain a website with census and voting data and interactive mapping software, and take public input before submitting a plan [S3].

A state could not redistrict again after its once-a-decade redistricting unless a court ordered it to comply with the Constitution or the Voting Rights Act, closing the door on mid-decade partisan remaps [S2][S3].

If a commission's plan is not enacted, the state's highest court would pick among commission-drawn plans, and if no state entity acts, a federal court would draw the plan — so legislators could not simply refuse to act and keep drawing maps themselves [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative majorities, whose parties lose control of drawing districts and whose safe seats become harder to engineer. Federal taxpayers would fund the commissions at $150,000 per House seat, roughly $65 million nationwide per decade [S3].

drawbacks.text: Commission members are appointed by the majority and minority leaders of the state legislature — the same party politicians the commission is meant to replace — so a well-timed appointment could still shape the mapmakers [S3].
The once-per-decade limit bars any redraw except court-ordered ones, so maps that advantage one party would stay locked in for the full ten years unless litigation succeeds [S3].
Federal payments of $150,000 per House seat are authorized for every multi-seat state, a recurring cost every ten years [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — maps drawn in public by people with no recent political career, ignoring party data and incumbent addresses — addresses the root of gerrymandering, and the fiscal cost is small. The main design weakness is that the appointment process still runs through the legislative leaders of both parties, so the commission's independence is partial rather than complete. On balance the bill would meaningfully reduce self-dealing in map-drawing, though it would not fully remove politicians from the process.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and later to a Constitution subcommittee, and it sat there until the two-year Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Cooper introduced the bill on January 4, 2021, the first day of the 117th Congress [S1][S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, and on March 1, 2021 was referred to the Subcommittee on the Constitution, Civil Rights, and Civil Liberties [S5].
No further action was taken before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023; the bill never received a hearing or a vote [S5].
The bill attracted only one cosponsor over its entire two-year life [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and the state legislative majorities of both parties who draw congressional maps kept that power, since no redistricting reform advanced in this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Incumbents who draw their own districts

for.name: Rep. Jim Cooper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 117th Congress

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jerry Nadler (D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; it sat in committee and subcommittee for the full two-year Congress

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor at any point in the Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and its single cosponsor were both Democrats, and no Republican signed on; but with only two total supporters, the record shows more indifference from both parties than a clear partisan fight.

industries.industry: Incumbent members of Congress and state legislative majorities of both parties
industries.note: The bill removes their power to draw the congressional districts they run in, ending the practice of legislators drawing maps that protect their own seats and their party's margins. Their interest in keeping that power runs directly against voters' interest in districts drawn without regard to party or incumbency.
